units.text: So what is Brussels now?
On paper, it is the Brussels-Capital Region, a territory of nineteen municipalities with about one and a quarter million people.
The City of Brussels, the historic center with the Grand Place, is only one of those nineteen.
The others have their own mayors and councils, and names that Brusselers use as proudly as the name of the city itself: Ixelles, Saint-Gilles, Schaerbeek, Anderlecht, Molenbeek, Uccle, and more.
The region is the capital of Belgium.
It is the capital of the Flemish Community and of the French Community.
And it is, informally but unmistakably, the capital of Europe.
The governance is a puzzle. Belgium is a federation of three regions and three language communities, layered on top of each other, and Brussels sits at the point where they all overlap.
The region's parliament has French-speaking and Dutch-speaking groups, and the government has to include members of both.
That sounds like a clever safeguard, and it is.
It also makes things slow. After regional elections in June of 2024, the parties could not agree on a coalition.
It took 613 days, more than twenty months, until a seven-party government finally took office in February of 2026, led by a French-speaking liberal, Boris Dilliès.
The parties had to promise to balance a budget that was deeply in deficit, and to merge various regional agencies.
For almost two years, the capital of Europe had run on a caretaker government.
At the national level, the story has been similar.
After elections in June of 2024, it took more than two hundred thirty days for a federal government to form.
In February of 2025, Bart De Wever, a Flemish nationalist who had long dreamed of a more independent Flanders, was sworn in as prime minister by King Philippe, in a five-party coalition.
It was the first time a Flemish nationalist had led the Belgian government, which is one of those ironies that Belgian history delivers regularly.
King Philippe, who succeeded his father Albert the Second in 2013, is the seventh king of the Belgians.
The real face of modern Brussels is its population.
On the first of January, 2025, the region counted about one million, two hundred fifty-six thousand people, and a bit over thirty-seven percent of them held a foreign passport.
That is not counting the many Belgians with a foreign background.
Residents come from about a hundred and eighty-three different nationalities.
The largest foreign group is French, followed by Romanians and Italians, then Spaniards and Moroccans.
Brussels also has an important Congolese community, centered on a district called Matongé.
In 2025, for the first time since the mid-1990s, the population stopped growing.
Many of those foreign residents work for the international institutions around which the modern city has grown.
The European Commission, the Council of the European Union, and parts of the European Parliament all have their seats here, around the Schuman roundabout and the Rue de la Loi.
NATO's headquarters, rebuilt in a striking new complex in the north of the city and opened in 2018, is in Brussels.
By the most recent count, more than fifty thousand people work for international institutions in the region.
Around them are embassies, trade associations, law firms, think tanks, and the lobbyists who try to influence the laws of the European Union.
Brussels, a city that once lived by cloth and tapestries, now lives largely by words and rules.
The city's recent history has also had dark days.

In November of 2015, after the terror attacks in Paris, some of whose planners had lived in the Brussels district of Molenbeek, the city went into a security lockdown that lasted days, with soldiers on the streets and the metro closed.
Then, on the eighteenth of March, 2016, police captured one of the key suspects, Salah Abdeslam, in Molenbeek.
Four days later, on the morning of the twenty-second of March, three suicide bombers struck.

Two bombs exploded in the departure hall of Brussels Airport at Zaventem, and an hour later, a third went off on a metro train leaving the Maalbeek station, in the heart of the European Quarter, right among the offices of the institutions.
Thirty-two people were killed, not counting the attackers, and more than three hundred were injured.
The Islamic State group claimed responsibility.
Every year since, the city has marked the anniversary, and the little statue of the Manneken Pis has been dressed in a firefighter's uniform to honor the rescuers.
The city has also been rethinking how it lives.

In 2015, the central boulevards around the Bourse were closed to cars, creating one of the largest pedestrian zones in Europe, and the old Boulevard Anspach, once built over the buried Senne, became a place for people to walk and sit.
A low-emission zone limits older cars, and a traffic plan called Good Move, which reduces through traffic in residential neighborhoods, has been bitterly debated.
Brussels is trying to become a city for people rather than just for commuters, and, like most such efforts, it is argued over fiercely.
And then there is the culture, which is as eclectic as the population.

Brussels is the capital of the comic strip, with dozens of giant murals of comic heroes painted on building walls across the city, a museum devoted to the art form, and a tradition that gave the world Tintin and the Smurfs.
It is a city of beer: in 2016, UNESCO recognized Belgian beer culture as part of the world's cultural heritage.

It is a city of chocolate. According to tradition, the praline, the filled chocolate, was invented in 1912 by a Brussels chocolatier named Jean Neuhaus, in the elegant glass-roofed Galeries Royales Saint-Hubert,
one of the oldest covered shopping arcades in Europe.
And it is a city of waffles, fries, and mussels, and of a small green vegetable that carries its name, the Brussels sprout, which was grown in the area around the city centuries ago.
The city is also reckoning with its past.

The Royal Museum for Central Africa, in Tervuren, which Leopold the Second built as a showcase of his colony, was closed for years and reopened in 2018 after a major renovation that tried to confront its colonial origins.
In 2020, during worldwide protests against racism, statues of Leopold the Second in Belgium were defaced, and some were removed.
A parliamentary commission examined Belgium's colonial past.
In 2022, King Philippe visited the Democratic Republic of the Congo and expressed deep regret for the suffering caused by colonial rule.
The debate is ongoing, and it will shape how the city understands itself in the years ahead.
If there is a symbol of the identity of Brussels, it is not a lion or a saint or a king.
It is a dog. In the local dialect, a zinneke is a mongrel, a mixed-breed street dog that belongs to no one breed.
Brusselers have adopted the word with affection for their city, a place of mixed languages, mixed origins, and mixed styles, where no one is quite purebred.
There is a small bronze statue of a dog, relieving itself against a post, on a street in the old center, and a colorful parade, held every two years, that celebrates the zinneke spirit.
So let's step back and look at the whole journey.
It began as a settlement in a marsh, with a chapel on an island.
It became a market town on the road between Flanders and Cologne, and a ducal capital.
Its guilds won a seat at the table.
It became the capital of the Burgundian and Habsburg Netherlands, the home of great painters and weavers.
It was nearly erased in 1695, and rebuilt in four years into one of the most beautiful squares in the world.
It passed from Spain to Austria to France to the Dutch, and in 1830, after a night at the opera and four days of street fighting, it became the capital of a new nation.
It grew rich under Leopold, on the profits of an empire built on terrible cruelty.
It was occupied twice, and spared the worst of two world wars.
And then, almost by accident, it became the working capital of a united Europe.
Through all of it, Brussels has been a place where different peoples and languages meet, argue, trade, and build together.
It has never had one identity, and perhaps that is its identity.
That is the story of Brussels.
Thank you for listening, and enjoy the city.
